# The Law {#sec-law}

The dumps and the design argument are the same conversation seen at two
distances.

Up close, R is a heap of tagged nodes, a generational collector, a
reference count, a promise, and a handful of objects that really are
mutable. From a package away, the useful question is which of your names
are allowed to be those mutable objects, and which names are facts that
must survive being passed around, printed, tested, and serialized.

Hold both distances at once and a law falls out. It is not an R law. It
is a law about programs that have to stay honest while the data is still
being discovered.

## Name it

A name is a decision that a concept exists.

`api_config` is a decision. `color` is a decision. `status_code` is a
decision if a bare integer would lie. The ubiquitous language Eric Evans described in *Domain-Driven Design*
for large domains is the same discipline scaled down to one package, or
one person's system: the words in the code, the words in the console, and
the words in your head are the same words, and you curate them. You do not inherit a vocabulary by subclassing someone else's
nouns. You write one, and you keep it small enough to defend.

Naming is also the encapsulation. A prefix, a package namespace, and a
stable verb are how a reader finds the operation. `api_config_new`,
`req_headers`, `format.foo` --- the module is the vocabulary, not a living
object you have to open to discover what it can do. Shells have worked
this way for decades. So do the R APIs that people actually love to call.

## Admit only valid values

A name that accepts anything is a comment.

The standard worth stealing is Alexis King's, from
[Parse, don't validate](https://lexi-lambda.github.io/blog/2019/11/05/parse-don-t-validate/):
construction *is* the check. Downstream code receives a value that already
means the name, and it stops re-asking. In a language with a real type
checker this is a theorem. In R it is a ritual you can house in an S3
constructor (`new_*`, `validate_*`, `as_*`) or in an S7 property and a
class validator. The housing is a tradeoff, discussed in
@sec-types. The requirement is not. If the work is production work, invalid
states are a bug at the boundary, not a vibe you check in the third method
that happens to care.

R will not make you do this. That is the whole difficulty, and it is also
why the REPL is such a good place to discover which names deserve the
ceremony. Discovery first. Then the parse.

## Show it well

A type is not done when it can be constructed. It is done when a human can
see what it means.

R already treats the console as a user interface: `print`, `format`,
`str`, and the semantic vocabulary in
[cli](https://cli.r-lib.org/). PowerShell went further and made the view
a separate, declarative contract
([format data](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.core/about/about_format.ps1xml),
sitting on the
[Monad manifesto](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/scripting/developer/monad-manifesto)'s
rule that the pipe carries objects and the host decides how they look).
The idea travels even though the XML does not. Skipping `format` is the
same kind of unfinished as skipping the validator: the value exists, and
nobody can read it.

Effects need the same courtesy. A warning, a progress meter, a verbose
trace, and a fatal error are different channels. Smashing them into
`cat()` throws away the only protocol R has for routing them. That
protocol is the condition system, and it is closer to
[Common Lisp](https://nhplace.com/kent/Papers/Condition-Handling-2001.html)
than the `tryCatch` habit suggests. @sec-signals goes into it.

## Extend it with verbs

The operation is the extension point.

R's generic-function tradition (S3, S4, S7) and the trait tradition in
[Rust](https://doc.rust-lang.org/book/ch10-02-traits.html) share a
posture: a new package can teach an old verb a new noun, or teach an old
noun a new verb, without owning the type's method table. Message-passing
objects invert the posture. The type owns the verbs, and extension leans
on subclassing or patching. Both are legitimate. They fit different
problems. Data work, HTTP, compilers, and tool-using models are usually
algebras --- verbs closed over types --- and they want the open verb.
Widgets, documents with identity, and long-lived sessions sometimes want
the closed object. R lets you build either, which is freedom and also how
a codebase loses the plot.

The practical shape that keeps showing up:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  data[Domain data] --> names[Names]
  names --> types[Values that admit only those names]
  types --> verbs[Verbs and generics]
  types --> views[Print, format, cli]
  verbs --> workflows[Workflows as composition]
  handles[Handles at the edge] --> workflows
  views --> host[The host]
```

Values in the middle. Handles at the rim, where identity is load-bearing:
a socket, a token that refreshes, a cache, a conversation. Verbs
everywhere a human or a pipe might call them. Views at the host.

## Two sentences, one book

Chambers compressed S and R into three principles, restated in
[*S, R, and Data Science*](https://journal.r-project.org/articles/RJ-2020-028/):
everything that exists is an object, everything that happens is a function
call, and interfaces to other languages are part of the language. The law
above is what those principles feel like when you are the one shipping the
package.

The metal chapters show why the value illusion holds, and where it is
contractually false. The hybrid chapters show why the language grew this
shape and why rigor feels like swimming upstream. The taste chapters are
the law applied: containers, runtime types, presentation, dispatch.

If you remember one recommendation, remember the split. Facts are values.
Capabilities are handles. Functions are the user interface. The console is
a view, not a leftover.
